clue.text: Plant herb so spreads around us

indicators.note: to go around something is to enclose it, so one piece sits inside the other
whatever spreads out is scattered and loses its original arrangement

parts.note: the letters taken as written, ready to be rearranged
taken as written

explanation.surface: A gardener watches a herb spread out until it surrounds the people tending it.
explanation.walkthrough: The six letters of HERB SO are rearranged into ROSEB_H, and US sits in the gap before the final H to give ROSEBUSH.
explanation.definitionFit: A rosebush is a shrub grown for its flowers, so it is a type of garden plant.

clue.text: Rapidly increase salad ingredient

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to shoot up, as prices do
second meaning: the peppery leaf Americans call arugula

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests salad sales booming, but the clue is two separate meanings of one word; rocket is the British name for arugula.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb it means climb very fast; as a noun it names the peppery leaf eaten in mixed green dishes.

clue.text: Work on article in distinctive phrase

parts.note: to slog is to work hard and steadily
the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A writer labours over a newspaper piece, hunting for a catchy turn of phrase.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Work on' reads as one phrasal verb, but 'on' just means the next piece follows; 'in' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: A slogan is a short memorable motto used in advertising or politics, a phrase made to stand out.

clue.text: Behind, cheer on from the terraces?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the bottom one sits on
second meaning, split in two: to support a team as a fan in the stands

explanation.surface: A fan in the stands shouts encouragement from behind the goal.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as two words, BACK SIDE is what a supporter does: back your side. Terraces are the standing areas of British football grounds; the question mark flags the split.
explanation.definitionFit: Behind as a noun is a polite word for the buttocks, and backside is its everyday synonym.

clue.text: Cook washes up

indicators.note: in a down entry, going up means reading from the bottom, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: to wet something is to wash it with water

explanation.surface: The chef who made dinner also does the washing up afterwards.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Washes up' reads as kitchen cleaning; split it, and 'up' turns the word for washes upside down in this down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: To stew is to simmer food slowly in liquid, one particular way to prepare a meal.

clue.text: Flower in university fed to reptiles

indicators.note: food that is fed to an animal ends up inside it

parts.note: short for crocodiles
U is the standard abbreviation for university

explanation.surface: A flower grown on campus is thrown to the crocodiles as feed.
explanation.walkthrough: The U goes inside CROCS, just before the final S.
explanation.definitionFit: The crocus is a small spring-blooming plant grown from a corm, with cup-shaped petals.

clue.text: Great queen's uplifting method

indicators.note: lifting a down entry upwards makes its letters read from bottom to top

parts.note: epic means grand or great in scale
ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the crossword queen

explanation.surface: A great queen has an inspiring way of doing things.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Uplifting' looks like praise for the queen's method, but it reverses EPIC + ER in this down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: A recipe is a set of instructions for achieving something, so a procedure or way of doing it.

clue.text: Riches he wasted in English county

indicators.note: something wasted is squandered and ruined, no longer in its original form

parts.note: the letters taken as written, ready to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A man squanders his fortune somewhere in the English countryside.
explanation.walkthrough: Cheshire is a county in north-west England, home of Cheshire cheese and the Cheshire Cat.
explanation.definitionFit: Cheshire is one of the administrative shires of England, bordering Wales and Greater Manchester.

clue.text: Comprehensive school's head in torment, it seems?

indicators.note: the head of a word is its very top, its opening letter

parts.note: the opening letter of the word
someone in torment would appear to be crying

explanation.surface: The head teacher of a comprehensive school looks as if they are suffering.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Comprehensive school' is a British state secondary school, but here the phrase is split: 'Comprehensive' is the definition and 'school' only lends its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Sweeping changes or statements are wide-ranging and all-embracing, which is what comprehensive means as an adjective.

clue.text: Note alien on part of one's trousers!

parts.note: the crotch is where the trouser legs meet
ET, the extra-terrestrial from the film

explanation.surface: A comic scene: a little alien is found sitting on a man's trousers.
explanation.walkthrough: In an across clue, 'on' means the second piece comes after the first; the exclamation mark flags the cheeky surface.
explanation.definitionFit: In British musical terminology a crotchet is a quarter note, one beat in common time.

clue.text: Plan to close off border in secret, oddly

indicators.note: one piece placed in another goes inside it
taking a word oddly means keeping only its first, third, fifth letters and so on

parts.note: the odd-numbered letters of the word
to hem is to fold over and sew a cloth edge so it will not fray

explanation.surface: A secret plan to shut off a frontier is hatched in a dark room.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Border' pretends to be a national frontier; together with 'close off' it describes finishing the edge of fabric. That goes inside SCE.
explanation.definitionFit: A scheme is a systematic plan or design for doing something, often with a hint of plotting.

clue.text: Plant seeds around room in flat

indicators.note: to go around something is to enclose it, so one piece sits inside the other

parts.note: to sow is to plant seeds
a hall is a large room

explanation.surface: Someone plants seeds in pots arranged around the room of their apartment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plant' looks like a noun and 'flat' like an apartment; both are misdirection, with 'Plant seeds' a single verb phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: A flat dish or tray has little depth, and shallow describes exactly that lack of depth.

clue.text: Pass back in game, then slip

indicators.note: the back of a word is its very end, its final letter

parts.note: the closing letter of the word
a lapse is a slip or small error

explanation.surface: A footballer passes the ball backwards during a match and then slips over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pass back' reads as a football back-pass, but 'Pass' is the definition and 'back in game' is the last letter of game.
explanation.definitionFit: When time elapses it goes by, which is the intransitive sense of pass, as in hours passing.

clue.text: Cut meat ASAP

parts.note: to chop is to cut
a chop is a cut of meat with the bone

explanation.surface: A butcher is told to slice the meat as soon as possible.
explanation.walkthrough: The same word appears twice, first as a verb and then as a noun. ASAP abbreviates 'as soon as possible'.
explanation.definitionFit: Chop-chop is an informal exclamation urging someone to hurry up, meaning quickly or immediately.

clue.text: Powerful unit — of artillery?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a cell that supplies electrical power
second meaning: a group of big guns, itself a military unit

explanation.walkthrough: The dash makes it look like one phrase about a strong military unit; it is really two meanings, a power cell and a set of guns.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both an electrical cell supplying power and an army unit of several heavy guns.

clue.text: I take my time quaffing last of ale, if possible

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: to quaff is to drink, and a drink ends up inside the drinker

parts.note: to dally is to dawdle or linger

indicators.note: the last of something is its final element, here the closing letter

parts.note: the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: A drinker says they like to linger over the end of their pint whenever they can.
explanation.walkthrough: The E goes inside DALLY after the D, and I stands in front.
explanation.definitionFit: Ideally, like 'if possible', introduces what one would prefer in the best circumstances.

clue.text: In the Navy singer?

definitions.note: describes a person, where the answer is a noun for that person
definitions.meaning: first meaning: a member of the Women's Royal Naval Service

explanation.walkthrough: The surface recalls the song 'In the Navy'. The Wrens were the British Women's Royal Naval Service, and a bird is a 'singer' in crosswords.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both a woman serving with the Royal Navy and a tiny brown songbird.

clue.text: Nuts — how to open them?

definitions.meaning: second meaning: the tools for breaking shells, the question mark flagging the playful sense

explanation.walkthrough: 'Them' points back to 'Nuts' read as food; the first definition uses 'Nuts' in the sense of mad.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is British slang for mad, and also the plural of the device used to break open shells.

clue.text: Tape in test case playing

indicators.note: letters that are playing are moving about freely, not staying in order

parts.note: the letters taken as written, ready to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A recording is played in court as evidence in a legal test case.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Playing' fits the tape in the surface, but it signals rearranging TEST CASE.
explanation.definitionFit: A cassette is a plastic case holding magnetic recording tape, commonly called a tape.

clue.text: Criminal ring uncovered by a pair of fools

indicators.note: uncovering something strips off its outer layer, so the edges come away

parts.note: A followed by two asses, an ass being a fool
the word loses its first and last letters

explanation.surface: A criminal gang is exposed by two bumbling idiots.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ring' pretends to be a gang, but it just loses its outer letters. The 'a' before the pair joins them: A + ASS + ASS.
explanation.definitionFit: An assassin is a murderer of a prominent person, so certainly a lawbreaker.

clue.text: Study money, having lost billion

indicators.note: something that has lost a part no longer contains it, so letters go

parts.note: bread is slang for money
B is the abbreviation for billion

explanation.surface: Someone studies their finances after losing a billion.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove the B from the slang word for money.
explanation.definitionFit: To read a subject is British usage for studying it at university, as in reading law.

clue.text: Figure incarcerated by brutal tsar if everything fails

indicators.note: a prisoner incarcerated is locked inside, so one piece goes within the other
something handled brutally is roughed up and knocked out of shape

parts.note: the letters taken as written, ready to be rearranged
a number is a figure

explanation.surface: A person jailed by a cruel Russian ruler, as a last resort.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Figure' could be a shape or a person, but here it is simply a number spelt out in full.
explanation.definitionFit: 'At worst' introduces the least favourable outcome, the case where every hope is disappointed.

clue.text: Put to death, the colour has drained from my skin

parts.note: my skin is the speaker's own, so the speaker says 'I am'
skin without colour looks pallid

explanation.surface: A condemned person goes white with terror at their execution.
explanation.walkthrough: Say what the clue describes in the first person: I'M PALE. The two pieces read as one word.
explanation.definitionFit: To impale is to pierce with a stake, historically a method of execution, so to kill someone.

clue.text: Crowd in front of room entertained by band

indicators.note: a guest entertained by a host is taken inside their home

parts.note: a thong is a narrow strip of leather, a band

indicators.note: the front of a word is where it starts, its opening letter

parts.note: the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: A crowd at the front of a hall is entertained by a pop group.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Band' is a group of musicians on the surface but a strap in the wordplay. R goes inside THONG.
explanation.definitionFit: A throng is a large densely packed mass of people, a synonym for a crowd.

clue.text: Road in Stockport cleared out, blocked by large plant

indicators.note: whatever blocks a passage sits inside it
a thing cleared out has its insides removed, leaving only the shell

parts.note: only the first and last letters remain
a tree is a large plant

explanation.surface: A road in Stockport is emptied because a fallen tree is blocking it.
explanation.walkthrough: Stockport is a town near Manchester. Keep its outer letters and put TREE between them.
explanation.definitionFit: A street is a public road in a town, lined with houses or shops.

clue.text: Choice other than plastic, simple material

parts.note: plastic means credit cards, so the other way to pay is notes and coins
mere means nothing more than, simple

explanation.surface: A shopper chooses between paying by card and paying for a simple fabric.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plastic' seems to be the material, but it means payment cards; the definition is the last word.
explanation.definitionFit: Cashmere is a fine soft wool from Kashmir goats, woven into luxurious fabric.

clue.text: Bag in a church possessed by Egyptian god

indicators.note: what is possessed by someone is held within their grasp

parts.note: Set was the Egyptian god of chaos and the desert
taken as written
CH is the standard abbreviation for church

explanation.surface: A bag found in a church is haunted by an ancient Egyptian deity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Possessed' suggests demonic haunting in the surface; in the wordplay it simply means held inside.
explanation.definitionFit: A sachet is a small sealed packet or pouch, holding sugar, shampoo or scented herbs.

clue.text: Firstly, dried eggs located in food shop

indicators.note: firstly points at the start, so each word gives its opening letter

parts.note: the opening letters of these four words

explanation.surface: Powdered eggs have been tracked down in a grocery store.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like a link to the definition, but it supplies the fourth letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Deli is short for delicatessen, a store selling cooked meats, cheeses and prepared dishes.

clue.text: Box in net smashed and hit

indicators.note: something smashed is broken apart, so its letters are thrown into disorder

parts.note: the letters taken as written, ready to be rearranged
a rap is a sharp blow

explanation.surface: A tennis player smashes a ball into the net, which is struck hard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Box in' reads as a place in the net, but it is the definition, a verb meaning trap.
explanation.definitionFit: To box someone in is to hem them in so they cannot escape, which is to catch or ensnare them.

clue.text: Jade, say, gets on with me when dancing

indicators.note: dancers move around and change places, so the letters do too

parts.note: the letters taken as written, ready to be rearranged
taken as written

explanation.surface: A woman called Jade gets along well with me on the dance floor.
explanation.walkthrough: Jade looks like a woman's name; with 'say' it is an example of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Jade is a green ornamental stone cut and polished for jewellery, one instance of a precious mineral.

clue.text: Feel the rage? Do that and stop driving!

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to become very angry
second meaning, taken literally: spot a red traffic light and halt

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is road-rage advice. 'Do that' points back at the phrase itself, read literally as noticing a red traffic signal.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to lose one's temper; literally, catching sight of a red signal obliges a motorist to halt.

clue.text: Dim thing blurred when it's dark

indicators.note: a blurred image has lost its clear shape, so the letters lose their order

parts.note: the letters taken as written, ready to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A faint object looks fuzzy once night has fallen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'When it's dark' seems to describe the dim thing, but it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Twelve o'clock at night is the middle of the night, a time of complete darkness.
